stories.headline: Update: Trump Administration Expands Ebola Travel Restrictions to Green Card Holders
stories.summary:
The Trump administration has broadened its Ebola-related travel restrictions to temporarily bar entry of lawful permanent residents — green card holders — who have been in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda, or South Sudan within the past 21 days. The move, announced by the Department of Health and Human Services and the CDC, marks a significant escalation of the administration's response to the ongoing Ebola outbreak in central Africa.

The expansion goes beyond earlier restrictions that targeted temporary visa holders and tourists. Immigration lawyers warn the change could affect hundreds of thousands of people and lead to family separations, as spouses or relatives may be stranded abroad while awaiting application decisions.

The announcement comes alongside a separate USCIS directive requiring most temporary visa holders already in the U.S. to return to their home countries to complete green card applications — a step critics say compounds legal immigration difficulties. Supporters of the restrictions argue the measures are necessary to prevent the spread of a deadly pathogen with no widely available treatment.

Public health officials are also contending with misinformation about the virus as cases continue to emerge in Africa. The administration has not indicated a specific end date for the restrictions, tying their duration to conditions on the ground in affected countries.

stories.headline: Update: Canadian PM Carney Calls Alberta 'Essential' as Province Sets October Separation Vote
stories.summary:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney pushed back Friday against Alberta separatism, calling the oil-rich western province 'essential' to Canada and praising its 'huge contributions' to the country. His remarks came one day after Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced citizens will vote October 19 on whether the province should remain in Canada or begin the legal process toward a binding independence referendum — framing the vote as a two-step process after a court ruling blocked direct action.

A First Nations-backed legal challenge earlier this month halted the verification of separation petition signatures, with the judge ruling Alberta's government failed to consult with indigenous communities. Smith said she would appeal the ruling but refused to let it silence Albertan voices. Smith herself said she will vote in favour of remaining in Canada, but defended holding the plebiscite on procedural grounds.

The vote represents the most significant test of Canadian national unity in decades. Critics from multiple directions panned the move: the Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation called Smith's government 'undemocratic and authoritarian,' NDP leader Naheed Nenshi called the vote 'needless,' and even separatist organizers expressed disappointment that the referendum fell short of a direct independence question. Opinion polls suggest roughly 25% of Albertans support independence.

Carney said his government is 'renovating the country' and that Alberta is central to that project, signaling Ottawa intends to address western grievances rather than dismiss them. The situation is being watched closely across Canada as a potential stress test for federal-provincial relations under a newly elected government.

stories.headline: Update: Cuban Government Holds Rally Outside U.S. Embassy in Defense of Raúl Castro
stories.summary:
The Cuban government organized a large rally outside the U.S. Embassy in Havana on Friday in defense of former president Raúl Castro, days after U.S. authorities indicted the 94-year-old on charges of conspiracy to kill U.S. nationals, murder, and destruction of aircraft stemming from the 1996 shootdown of two civilian planes operated by the exile group Brothers to the Rescue. Thousands of Cubans waved flags and chanted 'Long Live Raúl' at the demonstration; Castro did not appear in person.

Castro's daughter, Mariela Castro, was among those who spoke at the rally, which the government framed as a display of national solidarity against what Havana characterizes as politically motivated U.S. aggression. The indictment has drawn sharp condemnation from Cuban officials, who deny any wrongdoing and argue U.S. courts lack jurisdiction over the matter.

The charges mark a rare move by U.S. prosecutors to formally indict a former head of state for actions taken while in power, raising both legal and diplomatic questions about enforcement. With Castro living in Cuba and no extradition treaty in place, legal experts say any prosecution would be largely symbolic in practical terms but carries significant geopolitical weight.

The development comes as U.S.-Cuba relations remain severely strained, with Washington maintaining economic pressure on the island and Havana deepening ties with Russia and China. The rally signals the Castro-era leadership retains a degree of mobilization capacity despite Cuba's ongoing economic crisis.

stories.headline: Google's Search Overhaul Marks End of an Era as AI Reshapes the Internet
stories.summary:
Google this week announced what it called the 'biggest upgrade to our Search box in over 25 years,' accelerating a shift toward AI-generated responses that analysts say effectively closes the chapter on the early internet era of keyword-driven, link-based search. The overhaul replaces much of the traditional results page with AI summaries, raising questions about the future of web traffic for publishers and independent websites.

The change reflects a broader transformation of the digital landscape driven by generative AI and the so-called TikTok-ification of social media — platforms increasingly curated by algorithmic recommendation rather than user choice. Critics argue the shift concentrates information power in fewer hands and may undermine the open-web ecosystem that allowed diverse voices to reach audiences organically.

Proponents of the AI-driven model say it delivers faster, more relevant answers and reduces the friction of sifting through pages of links, many of which are cluttered with ads or SEO-optimized content of low quality. Google has framed the upgrade as a response to user demand and growing competition from AI-native search tools.

The redesign arrives as regulators in the U.S. and Europe scrutinize Google's dominance in search. The timing adds complexity to ongoing antitrust proceedings that have already found Google illegally maintained its search monopoly in the U.S., with remedies still being determined by a federal court.

stories.headline: Update: Senate Republicans Erupt at Acting AG Blanche Over $1.8 Billion 'Anti-Weaponization' Fund
stories.summary:
About half the Senate Republican Conference confronted acting Attorney General Todd Blanche at a closed-door Capitol meeting Thursday, with Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) describing the session as featuring "screaming" and "fireworks at an epic level." Cruz said he was surprised by the intensity of his colleagues' anger over a proposed $1.8 billion fund described as an "anti-weaponization" initiative within the Justice Department.

The confrontation marks a significant new development in Republican opposition to the fund, which the Senate GOP had already voted to strip from legislation earlier this week. Thursday's meeting escalated that friction into a direct, heated exchange between a senior Trump administration official and members of the president's own party in Congress.

The episode underscores deepening tensions between Senate Republicans and the Trump Justice Department over the fund's scope and purpose. Critics within the party have raised concerns about how the money would be used, while administration allies have framed it as a tool to counter politically motivated prosecutions. No resolution was announced following the meeting.

stories.headline: Update: U.S.-Cuba Tensions Deepen as Washington Signals Low Odds of Peaceful Resolution
stories.summary:
The United States and Cuba are locked in an escalating confrontation, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio declaring this week that the likelihood of a peaceful diplomatic agreement with Havana is "not high." Washington has imposed an oil blockade, new sanctions, and an unprecedented murder indictment against former Cuban leader Raúl Castro, while simultaneously increasing surveillance flights near the island — with military aircraft broadcasting their positions on public tracking sites in what experts describe as a deliberate show of force.

Cuba's Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez accused Rubio of trying to "instigate military aggression" and charged the U.S. with constructing a "fraudulent case" to justify intervention. U.S. news outlet Axios, citing classified intelligence, reported that Cuba possesses 300 drones and has discussed targeting nearby U.S. assets including Guantanamo Bay and naval vessels; Cuba denied posing any threat, saying it "neither threatens nor desires war."

The situation has deepened concerns about the possibility of U.S. military action in the Caribbean. The Trump administration has not announced any invasion plans, but President Trump has previously mused that Cuba is "ready to fall" and suggested the possibility of a "friendly takeover." Iranian military advisers may be present in Havana, according to U.S. intelligence cited by Axios, a claim Cuba has not directly addressed. Analysts note the rapid deterioration of relations since Trump returned to office represents a sharp break from the partial normalization pursued under the Obama administration.

stories.headline: Italian Cave Divers Lacked Proper Safety Equipment, Rescue Diver Reveals
stories.summary:
The Finnish diver who recovered the bodies of four Italian scuba divers from a deep underwater cave in the Maldives has said they were found without the standard safety equipment used in cave diving. Sami Paakkarinen told Italian media the divers lacked a scuba reel or guide rope — tools he described as essential for navigating such hazardous environments — and said the gear recovered with the bodies "was not optimal."

The five Italian divers, including two University of Genoa marine researchers, disappeared on May 14 after entering a 60-metre-deep cave in Vaavu Atoll during rough weather. Paakkarinen described the recovery site as "very deep" and "very challenging," and suggested the cause may have been "a tragic human error," though he deferred to investigators for a final determination. A Maldivian rescue diver, Staff Sgt. Mohamed Mahdhee, died during the search operation.

The four recovered bodies are expected to be repatriated to Italy on Saturday, where post-mortem examinations will be conducted. The accident is considered the worst single diving incident in Maldivian history. Italian authorities are expected to open an inquiry into the circumstances of the dive.

stories.headline: Nearly 40 Million Americans Expected on Roads for Memorial Day Weekend Despite Four-Year High Gas Prices
stories.summary:
AAA estimates nearly 40 million Americans will travel by road this Memorial Day weekend, a figure that would set a new record, even as gas prices reach their highest levels in four years. The surge in travel is occurring against the backdrop of broader consumer strain, with elevated fuel costs cutting into household budgets across the country.

The holiday travel outlook comes as economic analysts have flagged signs of a consumer slowdown driven in part by persistent energy costs. Despite those pressures, demand for holiday travel appears resilient, with air and road bookings both running strong heading into the long weekend.

Memorial Day weekend traditionally marks the unofficial start of summer travel season in the United States, making the volume of travelers a closely watched indicator of consumer confidence and discretionary spending. Transportation officials are advising drivers to expect significant congestion on major highways beginning Friday afternoon.

stories.headline: Update: Pentagon Releases Second Batch of UFO Files, Including Senior Intelligence Officer's 2025 Account
stories.summary:
The Pentagon on Friday released a second batch of declassified UFO files, including 51 videos, audio recordings, and a half-dozen documents spanning 80 years of sightings. The materials follow an initial release of 161 files on May 8, ordered by President Trump, who encouraged the public to draw their own conclusions.

A notable new document contains a first-hand account from an unnamed senior U.S. intelligence officer who reported witnessing "countless orange orbs swarming in all directions" from a military helicopter in 2025 over the western United States. The officer described oval-shaped, super-hot objects moving at high speed that coalesced into a triangle formation before vanishing, an encounter lasting more than an hour.

Other materials include a 116-page Armed Forces Special Weapons Program report from 1948–1950 documenting 209 sightings at Sandia, New Mexico, and videos captured by U.S. military infrared cameras between 2018 and 2023. The Pentagon cautioned that many videos lacked a verified chain of custody, meaning they could have been altered.

No definitive conclusions about extraterrestrial life or alien technology were drawn in the files. U.S. officials stated the public could interpret the materials as they saw fit.

stories.headline: Senegal's President Faye Sacks Prime Minister Sonko, Dissolves Government
stories.summary:
Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye on Friday abruptly dismissed Prime Minister Ousmane Sonko and dissolved the country's government, ending a political partnership that had brought the two men to power together just over a year ago. A presidential decree read on national television ended Sonko's duties and those of all ministers and state secretaries.

The split follows months of public tension between the two leaders. Sonko had openly criticized Faye during a parliamentary session earlier this week, accusing the president of a "failure of leadership," while Faye had reportedly rebuked Sonko for "excessive personalisation" within their ruling Pastef party. Sonko responded to his dismissal on social media, writing he would "sleep with a light heart."

The political crisis comes as Senegal faces severe economic strain. The country's public debt stands at 132 percent of GDP according to the IMF, which has frozen a $1.8 billion lending program with the country. Hundreds of students demonstrated in the capital Dakar in support of Sonko following Tuesday's parliamentary session.

Sonko, a popular figure among Senegalese youth, had been barred from the 2024 presidential election due to a defamation conviction and backed Faye's successful bid instead. The two had run under the joint slogan "Diomaye is Sonko, Sonko is Diomaye." No replacement prime minister has been announced.

stories.headline: Update: GOP Senator Floats Elise Stefanik to Replace Gabbard as Director of National Intelligence
stories.summary:
Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.) on Friday publicly suggested Rep. Elise Stefanik (R-N.Y.) as a candidate to succeed Tulsi Gabbard as Director of National Intelligence, calling her "easily confirmable" and saying she would make a great replacement. Gabbard resigned the post earlier this week following her husband's cancer diagnosis.

Separately, reporting identified Aaron Lukas, a former CIA officer, as the figure selected to replace Gabbard in an acting or interim capacity. Lukas is described as aligned with some of President Trump's core intelligence-community critiques, including the view that agencies have been infiltrated by ideological bias and skepticism toward the Russia-2016 election narrative.

The DNI vacancy is significant given the role's central function in coordinating the U.S. intelligence community. Any permanent nominee would require Senate confirmation, making confirmability a key factor in the selection. Stefanik, currently serving in the House, was previously nominated as U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations before that nomination was withdrawn.

The White House has not officially announced a permanent successor. The jockeying over the position reflects broader tensions within the Republican Party over the direction of the intelligence community under the Trump administration.

stories.headline: France's 2027 Presidential Race Takes Shape as Former PM Philippe Emerges as Early Favourite
stories.summary:
With roughly one year until France's next presidential election, former Prime Minister Édouard Philippe has emerged as the leading centrist candidate and the figure polls suggest is most capable of defeating a hard-right opponent in the second round. Philippe, 55, heads the small Horizons party and has begun formally organizing his campaign, announcing three campaign directors and adopting the Gaullist slogan "France Libre."

Opinion polls consistently show Philippe as the only candidate able to beat either Marine Le Pen or her deputy Jordan Bardella of the National Rally in a runoff. In any other polled matchup, a populist-right candidate would win, raising alarm among centrist and European-aligned political circles. Le Pen's eligibility to run remains subject to legal proceedings.

Philippe faces competition from within the centrist and center-right space, including former Prime Minister Gabriel Attal of Macron's Renaissance party, who declared his candidacy Friday, and conservative Bruno Retailleau. France's two-round voting system penalizes vote-splitting heavily, placing pressure on rival centrist candidates to eventually consolidate behind a single figure.

Philippe is leaning right on economic policy, favoring a further increase in the retirement age beyond 64 and constitutionally mandated balanced budgets. He plans a mass "apartment meeting" beamed into 1,000 French homes in June and his first formal rally in Paris on July 5.
